html:
The Battle of Tel el-Kebir was fought on 13 September 1882 in the eastern Nile delta of Egypt, about 110 km northeast of Cairo. A British army under Garnet Wolseley beat the Egyptian army of Ahmed Urabi in about an hour.

Egypt was deep in debt to European lenders, and Britain and France controlled its finances. Urabi, an army colonel, led a movement against the khedive and foreign control; see the Urabi revolt. Britain feared for its loans and for the Suez Canal, its short route to India. After riots in Alexandria, the British fleet shelled the city in July 1882. Wolseley then seized the canal and landed at Ismailia. Urabi dug in at Tel el-Kebir to block the road to the capital. Wolseley marched about 13,000 men across the desert at night, guided by the stars, and attacked at dawn. The British lost 57 dead, the Egyptians perhaps 2,000.

British cavalry rode into Cairo the next day. Urabi was tried and exiled to Ceylon. Britain said its stay would be short, but its last troops left only in 1956, the year of the Suez Crisis. Egypt became part of the British Empire in all but name.
